summary: The video side is built as one 007121-style chip module. It fetches tiles and sprites per scanline into line buffers, chooses tile or sprite per pixel with a priority mux, runs both colours through 4-bit lookup PROMs, outputs a 7-bit colour code and derives interrupts from raster-counter bits. That is a different breakdown from MAME, which splits the work into driver tilemap callbacks, clip rectangles and draw-order layering. The 051733 math chip is the exception: it is a behavioural register-file model that uses MAME's operand names and read-switch layout, and it computes results arithmetically rather than from chip logic. Timing comes from a generic framework timer, and there is no gate- or counter-level detail, so the core leans hardware but is not strongly board-derived.

findings.signal: Tilemaps, priority and PROM lookup kept inside the video-chip module
findings.note: The chip module itself combines tiles and sprites and drives a 7-bit output {pal_bank, tile/obj select, 4-bit PROM data}. In MAME, the tilemap decode, palette indirection and layering all sit in driver functions outside the k007121 device.

findings.signal: Per-pixel priority mux instead of draw-order layering
findings.mame_ref: labyrunr.cpp:screen_update (tilemap0 cat0 -> sprites -> tilemap0 cat1 -> tilemap1)
findings.note: scr_sel = obj_blank || no_obj || tile_prio || txt_line, worked out each pixel from the line-buffer outputs. MAME gets the same effect by drawing whole layers in order with categories and a priority bitmap.

findings.signal: Single scanline tile fetcher, text columns as a second pass
findings.note: One HS-triggered fetch engine reads attr/code VRAM, then the ROM, then the line buffer. In the wide layout it makes a second 'scores' pass over the left text columns. MAME instead uses two separate tilemap objects with clip rectangles and scroll offsets.

findings.signal: Tile bank bits picked by mux select
findings.note: Each code bit is attr_scan[3+codeN_sel], overridden by extra_bits under extra_mask, written as a per-bit 4:1 mux. MAME builds the bank with chained shift/mask arithmetic and a final mask merge.

findings.signal: Interrupts from raster-counter bits and a toggle flip-flop
findings.note: NMI fires on rising edges of vdump[4] or vdump[5]. FIRQ comes from a flip-flop that toggles on each IRQ release. MAME uses a 16-line timer callback, a scanline mask test and frame_number()&1.

findings.signal: Per-line sprite scan with its own limits, not MAME's block count
findings.note: Each line, the sprite table is walked byte by byte (attr 4, y 2, code 0, colour 1, x 3) with a vertical range check. The ROM address is built from code bits and vsub, and the walk ends at a 384-pixel budget, a 0x13b table limit or y==240. MAME pre-counts 264 sprite blocks, then draws whole sprites with x_offset/y_offset tables.

findings.signal: Sprite page latched at VBL, not a buffered copy of the list
findings.note: Only the obj_page select bit is latched on vdump[8], and sprites are read live from RAM. This departs from MAME's memcpy sprite buffer, but it is not clearly board-derived either.

findings.signal: Palette RAM read as two bytes per pixel
findings.note: An 8-bit palette RAM is addressed with {gfx_pxl, ~pal_half} and read twice per pixel at the doubled pixel clock, with the bytes shifted together into a 15-bit colour. That is how an 8-bit-wide palette RAM behind the chip's colour code would work, unlike MAME's indirect palette entries.

findings.signal: 051733 as a behavioural model using MAME's operand names
findings.note: A 32-byte register file is decoded into op1/op2/op3/rad and the y1,x1,y2,x2 object coordinates in MAME's order and with MAME's names. Reads go through a case on the address returning div/mod/sqrt/collision values computed arithmetically (pipelined divider, binary-search sqrt), not through chip-like logic. Its RNG and collision results differ from this MAME version.

findings.signal: Generic framework timer and clip constants
findings.note: Raster timing comes from jtframe_vtimer with chosen parameters, not the chip's own H/V counters. Render start points and borders (octal 050, 020, 030, 410, 420) match MAME's screen geometry constants, which any correct core would share.

findings.signal: Address decode is the memory map
findings.note: Decoding uses A[15:11] compares and a case on A[10:8], similar to a 3-to-8 decoder, plus a 3-bit bank latch. It is the same map MAME has, so it is evidence neither way.
